data.content_ref: inline:The target's claim asserts we prefer corroborated theories because 'they have been error-tested and found wanting in fewer ways, making them the best available targets for further elimination of error.' This stated criterion is self-defeating. 'Found wanting' means 'found to be deficient or flawed.' A theory that has never been tested has been 'found wanting' in zero ways — no tests have been conducted, so no deficiencies have been discovered. By the target's own criterion ('fewer ways found wanting = better'), a completely untested theory would rank as preferable to any tested theory that has revealed even a single weakness. This inverts the very preference the target is trying to defend. The target's mechanism compounds the error by saying untested theories are 'known to be even more risky,' but on the target's own stated epistemic criterion (fewer ways found wanting), the untested theory is epistemically superior — it has zero recorded deficiencies. The criterion thus either collapses into triviality (it cannot distinguish between a theory that survived rigorous testing and one that was never examined) or actively favors the untested, directly contradicting the Popperian preference it purports to defend. Unlike prior objections about induction-smuggling in action, this objection targets the internal logical coherence of the target's own stated selection criterion: the metric 'found wanting in fewer ways' does not and cannot yield the preference the target claims it does.
